title: The True Story Behind 'Madden' and the Video Game that Turbo-Charged the NFL
author: Sean Gregory
body:
In 1984, Trip Hawkins, founder of video-game publisher Electronic Arts (EA), boarded an Amtrak train in Denver for a meeting that would one day prove monumental. He walked into the dining car to pitch John Madden, the CBS football commentator and omnipresent commercial spokesman who famously feared flying, on lending his name to a football video game Hawkins wanted to create.

Hawkins explained to Madden that there was just one hitch. Since the 8-bit home consoles of that era did not have the technological capability to replicate an actual 11-vs.-11 NFL game, Hawkins proposed that Madden support a 7-vs.-7 version of football. Madden, who won a Super Bowl as coach of the Oakland Raiders in 1977 and grew even more famous explaining the intricacies of trench warfare at the line of scrimmage to millions of viewers—through exhortations like “BOOM!” and “BAM!”—responded that a watered-down version of football, without a bunch of broad-shouldered linemen slamming into one another, was unacceptable.

“He just looked at me and said, ‘That's not real football,” Hawkins tells TIME. “He's always going to do that. He's going to just look you in the eye, he's going to be deadly serious, he's going to speak with his even tone, and it's going to be like the voice of God. And you're going to do exactly what he says.”

The creation of the Madden video game franchise, one of the best-selling sports titles in history, is covered in the third act of David O. Russell’s new sports drama Madden, which comes out on Nov. 18, in limited theaters and streaming on Prime Video. The film, starring Nicholas Cage as Madden and Christian Bale as Al Davis, the mercurial owner of the Raiders who was Madden’s former boss and close friend, also dives into Madden's coaching career, including his struggles balancing his passion for the game with attending to his family—Kathryn Hahn shines as Madden’s wife, Virgina—plus his transition into broadcasting. After becoming lead football commentator for CBS in 1981—he later joined FOX, ABC, and NBC—Madden’s exuberant analysis of NFL games and everyman persona made him ubiquitous in American culture, including during commercial breaks, through his ads for Miller Lite, Ace Hardware, Tinactin, and other products.

But the scenes concerning the video game, with comedian John Mulaney portraying Hawkins, stand out, as they shed light on one of the more underexplored, though arguably most important, aspects of his legacy. The Madden game’s success fed into the 21st century growth of the NFL, which is the undisputed king of American sports: many fans of the game, particularly young kids, grew into diehard fans of the league, and vice versa. And though Madden retired as a commentator in 2009, and passed away in 2021, his name will live on, very likely into perpetuity, through a game shaped by his vision.

Russell, Madden’s co-writer and director who is also a producer on the film, was struck by his teenage son’s experience playing the game. So he wanted to tap into its birth in the movie. “It was a revelation to me how this was this campfire, or street corner, through which he and his friends hung out,” says Russell. “I saw his joking and dancing, and it was a whole side of him that came to life from playing this game.”

Football fans may notice that the film casts two NFL players, star running back Marshawn Lynch and wide receiver Julian Edelman, in roles as nerdy video-game programmers. “If you talk to anyone under 40, the question would be, who didn’t play Madden?” says Edelman, who won three Super Bowls with the New England Patriots and was named MVP of Super Bowl LIII, in 2019. “It’s given people the language to be able to communicate football.” Edelman, 40, would play Madden for hours on Friday nights with friends he grew up with in the Bay Area. “You got to be your favorite professional football player,” says Edelman. “I got to be Jerry Rice. I got to be Steve Young. I got to be Jeff Garcia. You started to be able to create a player, or you got to play with old teams like the ‘88 Niners. You got to play with Roger Craig and all these guys. It just inspired you because you wanted to be those guys.”

A thrill for any young NFL player is seeing yourself featured in the game. Edelman says he threw “thousands” of passes to himself, every game, while controlling Tom Brady in Madden. “I would try to juice up all my stats before I was getting the rock from Brady,” he says. “The only action I was getting was in Madden.”

According to Russell, Lynch—nicknamed “Beast Mode”—ribbed him for wearing an Edelman jersey to set one day. Lynch’s Seahawks famously lost the Super Bowl to Edelman’s Patriots in 2015, when Seattle called for a pass play, from the one-yard line, instead of handing the ball off to Beast Mode to stuff into the end zone for the winning late-game score. Malcolm Butler of the Patriots picked off Russell Wilson’s pass, clinching New England its first Super Bowl victory in a decade. “Marshawn walks up to me an inch from my face and goes. ‘What is that? Why are you wearing that?’” says Russell, who has received five Oscar nominations for his directing and writing work on The Fighter, Silver Linings Playbook, and American Hustle. “I'm like, ‘I thought it would be nice for Julian. Is it OK?’ He goes, ‘It’s diabolical.’”

Madden takes a bit of dramatic license. In the film, Mulaney-as-Hawkins first pitches Madden at the Super Bowl victory party, in 1977, after his Raiders dispatched the Minnesota Vikings. That never happened: Hawkins first met Madden on the 1984 Amtrak. “I wanted to get him going in the story,” Russell says of the Hawkins character. “There’s feature filmmaking then there’s documentaries. In feature filmmaking, you want to meet a character that foreshadows your future.”

The movie leaves out Hawkins’ athletic background: he was far from a total football bumpkin. He played on the freshman football team at Harvard. But an audience doesn’t need to know that: there’s more tension, and comic opportunities, when worlds collide. “They didn't speak each other's language,” says Mulaney of his character and Cage’s Madden. “When you put someone like me in there, it's a good signal to the audience: this might not be a guy who's always in the huddle.”

In the film, Davis plays a role in helping EA and Madden secure a license, from the NFL, to use team names and logos in the game. But Davis was a longtime league nemesis with a penchant for filing lawsuits against fellow owners. “Al Davis,” says Hawkins, “had nothing to do with that.”

The gist of the Madden game arc: Hawkins, who left Apple in 1982 to start EA, first wanted Joe Montana, the Hall of Fame quarterback who won four Super Bowls with the San Francisco 49ers, as the game’s namesake. But Montana had a deal with Atari, the early-‘80s video-game juggernaut, to promote its products. “I thought, oh shoot, I can't do it with my hero, so never never mind,” says Hawkins, who cheered for the Niners in the Bay Area. “I don't want to do it with anybody else.”

Hawkins turned his attention to launching a basketball game—One on One: Dr. J vs. Larry Bird—before returning to football. He thought he could pay a coach to help him finish the design of the game, then worry about the name later: Hawkins met with former Minnesota Vikings quarterback and Cal football coach Joe Kapp. “We had a great meeting, and he was excited,” says Hawkins. “And then a couple days later he said, ‘I changed my mind. I want my name on the game, and I want royalties on the game.’” Joe Kapp Football wouldn’t fly.

But could the game thrive with another name on the box? “I thought, ‘Well, OK, if I'm going to have to pay anybody royalties, who do I want to pay them to?” says Hawkins. “And then, bing, instantly in my mind, it's John Madden.” By this time, Madden was starring in Miller Lite commercials and had hosted Saturday Night Live. But Madden’s insistence on 11 vs. 11 delayed the game’s development, to the point where some EA execs had a nickname for Hawkins’ football project: Tripp’s Folly.

But it did eventually debut, in 1988, on the Apple II. Once John Madden Football got on the Sega Genesis, an upstart home console competitor to the Nintendo Entertainment System, in 1990, it was game on. Madden had turned over one of his playbooks to EA to help make the game more sophisticated: in 1993, Madden NFL ‘94 was released on both the Sega Genesis and Super NES, with league-licensed team logos and names. It became a best-seller. The next year, actual player names were included.

Since 1995, “Madden Bowl” tournaments have taken place during Super Bowl week, bringing together celebrities and e-sports talents to play and promote the game. In August 2026, EA—which in addition to the Madden series has published the globally popular FIFA soccer franchise, a college football game, and non-sports titles like The Sims series—closed its sale to a consortium of investors for $55 billion, the largest-ever buyout funded by private equity. NFL revenue has jumped from some $4 billion in 2000 to more than $23 billion in 2025.

Hawkins stepped down as CEO of EA in 1991, and stayed on as board chair until 1994. He has since founded other game companies and worked as an executive coach, speaker, and startup advisor. He sold more than $65 million worth of EA stock in the 1990s. Hawkins also has first-hand insight into a beloved figure—and subject of the new film—who explained football to the masses. “From my perspective, from spending hours and hours alone in a room with him, the guy’s a classic nerd, and a classic introvert,” says Hawkins. “But then he also knows how to lead. You realize pretty quickly, yeah, this guy can tell 60 very large humans on an NFL team what to do, and get them to do it.” And millions more, of all sizes, to pick up a controller and call a play.
